articleTitle: Current limiting arc flash quenching system for improved incident energy reduction
abstract: In response to a growing concern to mitigate arc flash incident energy hazards, the latest edition of the National Electric Code NFPA70-2017 includes requirements for reducing clearing time of overcurrent protective devices with a continuous current rating of 1200A or higher. Section 240.87 lists seven options for reducing arc fault energy. This paper will briefly review the defined methods of reducing incident energy as outlined in the Standard, with focus on option 4: energy-reducing arc flash mitigation systems.

articleTitle: Digital transformation of the global cement industry
abstract: Major challenges facing the cement industry today include cost reductions, environmental protection and energy and capital efficiency. The best way to confront these challenges and to improve operational excellence is for the industry to embrace technological advances and innovations - many already proven in other industries - and not just to focus on technological optimization of old techniques. Such technological advances, often discussed today under the title the “Internet of Things” (IoT), include but are not limited to issues such as end-to-end process automation and instrumentation, the use of engineering and application software for the entire plant lifecycle phase and the employment of software platforms that collect, analyze and display data from various sources either from within an individual plant or across several plants. The data acquired in the field must be securely transported across the network, safely stored - possibly in a cloud - and intelligently analyzed and displayed in dashboards. Data sources can include enterprise resource planning (ERP), data warehouses, production databases, document management systems, process historians, and manufacturing data. With this customized and easy-to-understand real-time information at their fingertips, decision-makers and plant managers are in a position to make more informed, actionable decisions about their resources, their assets, their employees, their suppliers and their customers. The result is improved asset utilization and optimized customer and supplier relationships.

articleTitle: Considering the benefits of retrofitting centrifugal fan rotors
abstract: An understanding of how different flow control methods (inlet dampers vs. VFDs) affect a fan's efficiency and plant operating costs will be discussed. Case studies are considered to provide an understanding of the required data and eligibility for pursuing fan efficiency retrofits. Opportunities for retrofit are generally practical when there are oversized fans, process changes, or when there is equipment addition to the system. Benefits of energy efficiency retrofits can be predicted from field studies and an ROI is determined. Whether or not fan casing, ductwork, and existing motors and motor components can be reused is considered in the cost analysis. Also, there are generally rebates and incentives from local utilities can contribute to funding to assist with providing the necessary return on investment. In this paper, predicted ROI is compared to actual field results.

articleTitle: Optimized kiln operation by keeping kiln shell temperatures at set point with controlled water cooling
abstract: The increasingly powerful and sophisticated kiln firing process conditions make it necessary to cool the kiln shell in order to protect the refractory material and the steel body from overheating and wear. Traditionally the cooling is done with high performance blowers and only a few plants in the world are actually working more or less successfully with cooling by water evaporation. In 2014 a team consisting of the VDZ and a Cement Manufacturer, decided to conduct as an expert in measurement and control technologies. The aim was to develop an efficient cooling system with the medium of water. The goal was to determine at first how much water is needed to produce not an equivalent cooling effect as achieved with a conventional cooling fan. Advantages of the water cooling are obvious: Higher cooling effect Electrical energy consumption is very low Opportunity to cool a more precise point or region Low noise emissions. To accomplish a precise and robust control for the amount of water, a control unit was constructed by the supplying company, which has extensive monitoring mechanisms. Besides monitoring the kiln shell temperature using an infrared pyrometer, the amount of water per nozzle and the water pressure of the four separate cooling units are constantly checked. According to a freely selectable desired value (target temperature) for each cooling unit, the respective water nozzle is only supplied with water via a solenoid valve while the reference value is exceeded. Each of the 4 cooling units is thus adapted to the ideal kiln shell temperature and is therefore only spraying water on the local area, as long as it is above the target temperature. The selective cooling of a very hot local area even offers the opportunity to reduce the extreme stress to the surrounding area, thereby preventing excessive stretching, which is particularly advantageous for the refractory material. Within more than 20 installations world-wide operators confirm that it was possible to extend the kiln operation using the patented system for several weeks-sometimes months, so that they could avoid an unplanned kiln stop due to furnace hot spots. The following article describes the system developed by a German measurement and control company together with a Cement Producer and the German Cement Producers Association and shows case studies from all over the world.

articleTitle: CO2 capture from cement manufacture and reuse in concrete
abstract: A technology has been developed that utilizes CO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub> in concrete curing to improve the concrete properties. This process has been commercialized and is in use in over 50 ready mix and concrete product sites across the United States and Canada. At the current time ready mix and concrete product companies are using commercial, food grade CO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub> at a high cost. The long term objective is to extract CO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub> from cement plants and then utilize that same CO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub> in ready mix concrete and concrete products made with the cement that produced the CO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub>, thus closing the loop. This concept has been presented as one of many projects in the Carbon XPrize and has been selected as one of 27 projects approved for round 2. This XPrize team has selected cryogenic carbon capture as the best solution for extracting CO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub> from cement plant exhaust streams. The cryogenic capture technology has already been trialed at one US cement plant. Lab testing on a simulated exhaust gas stream has already been completed for XPrize validation. A second cement plant CO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub> extraction trial, using cryogenic capture is scheduled for January, 2018. This paper will discuss the two technologies; CO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub> usage in concrete curing and the cryogenic capture of CO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">2</sub> from a cement plant exhaust gas stream. The paper will discuss the basics of the Carbon XPrize submissions and status. The future of both technologies and the consequences for the cement and concrete industries will be explored further in the paper.

articleTitle: Pursuing a lower total cost of ownership in a large kiln baghouse
abstract: Cement plant operators have the never ending challenge of balancing the production requirements of their plants with ongoing maintenance, environmental compliance, energy consumption and overall plant profitability. This paper will highlight a demonstration performed at a US cement plant over the past year comparing and evaluating different types of filter media including a newly innovated low drag filter media. The goal of the demonstration was aimed at simultaneously increasing overall performance of the main air pollution control kiln baghouse while ensuring environmental requirements and build a case for a decrease in the Total Cost of Ownership of operating their main baghouse. The low drag filter demonstration has operated for over a year and has exceeded the initial performance expectations. The demonstration plan along with the performance data from the past year will be discussed.

articleTitle: Modular grinding stations (MGS) for sustainable growth
abstract: Cement Industry is changing the business paradigm, searching for scaled ways of growth, controlling risks and avoiding high investments. Modular Grinding Stations (MGS) are an innovative solution that allows Cement Producers to improve their scheduling and business intelligence. MGS in Cement Industry has had Momentum since 2011. This matured technology - proven worldwide and improved year over year - is evolving to larger sizes and offering a wide range of possibilities. All the Project Management Stages (Engineering, Procurement, Construction and Operation) are being designed into a virtuous retrofit circuit, with the result of Standardization. Standardized Installations are minimizing Capex deviations and on-site erection costs. MGS have also introduced the concept of Relocatable Installations. Having moveable assets, makes the decision taking easier, shortens the time in the market of production facilities and eases financing and permitting. This technical paper tries to show the advantages and challenges of this MGS technology, showing real case scenarios that illustrate the potentiality of this innovation.

articleTitle: Automated baghouse troubleshooting diagnostics maximize efficiency
abstract: Automated baghouse troubleshooting systems assure optimized filtration efficiencies to minimize particulate emissions for a cleaner, safer, healthier and compliant workplace. This paper also reviews a secondary benefit that is often overlooked. These same technologies also reduce baghouse operating and maintenance costs converting a perceived EPA or OSHA expense into a real and relatively quick return on investment “ROI” project. Integrating particulate, pressure, temperature and other process sensors into a pulse-jet baghouse cleaning control program provides several real-world benefits. Early-warning diagnostic alarms that result save time and money and prevent escalating problems by immediately identifying: 1. Filter leaks by row 2. Failed solenoids by row 3. Leaking or problematic diaphragm valves by row 4. Low compressed air supply 5. Problematic differential pressure (DP) levels 6. High temperature levels 7. Other process conditions adversely impacting efficiency and safety. Diagnostic automated baghouse troubleshooting technology is installed in the cement industry demonstrating the following five specific areas of cost containment that are reviewed in this paper. 1. Increase runtime between bag failures 2. Minimize maintenance and associated labor costs 3. Reduce filter replacement and disposal costs 4. Decrease compressed air and energy consumption 5. Assure a cleaner, safer, more compliant and healthier workplace.

articleTitle: Beneath our feet
abstract: Storage silos are vital to the operations of a cement manufacturing plant as well as to most terminal facilities. Reinforced concrete silos can provide decades of reliable service to owners, but routine inspection is recommended as part of a preventive maintenance program to ensure silos deliver dependable storage. Typically, reinforced concrete silos, either individual silos or groups of silos, have roofs that are constructed of reinforced concrete roofs that are supported by the perimeter concrete walls as well as by discrete structural steel beams that span from silo wall to silo wall. Silo designers in the past have traditionally not spent a great deal of time analyzing the bearing area of these steel beams on the walls. This has led to many, many issues with existing silos. Inspections in the past five years, since the catastrophic failure in 2012 that brought this long standing issue to the fore, have revealed that a large number of facilities have at least some silos with roof support beam bearing issues. Based on statistical information tabulated from the author's past inspections of facilities at eight major cement manufacturing companies, more than two out of every three facilities, including both terminals and plants, had multiple silos with significant deterioration at the roof support beam bearing areas. Although several repeated issues have been discovered during silo structural inspections, this presentation specifically focuses on roof support beam bearing issues. Deteriorated roof support beam bearing areas can lead to a loss of support of the silo roof slab. With the loss of support, the roof slab structure is compromised, and could fall right from under our feet. The deteriorated beam bearing issues can be a result of several different factors, including asymmetric flow, differential settlement of foundations, use of interstices for storage, pneumatic pressures used for filling of silos, and others. There are options for the inspection of these roof support beam bearing areas. Each has a level of accuracy, duration of inspection, effect on operations, and cost. The inspection of roof support beam bearing areas can be laborious, and must be done safely. It often requires a confined space permit, and it is recommended that the inspection be performed by an engineer experienced with silo design, construction, behavior, and inspection so that reliable conclusions and recommendations are provided to the owner. Repairs to these areas should consider the root cause of the problem, and typically allow for greater movement between the roof support beam and the silo wall. This paper will discuss: 1. The reality of roof support beam bearing area deterioration 2. Some of the causes of the deterioration 3. Different options for interior inspection of roof support beam bearing areas 4. Typical repair details to include 5. A number of helpful tips for owners to seek during plant walk downs.

articleTitle: Methods for quantifying rotor condition in synchronous motors
abstract: Synchronous motors play a key role in the operation of a large cement and aggregate facility. Advancement in the operating practices of the industry tends towards predictive maintenance and increasing time between planned outages. As end users extend the continuous duty-cycle of their synchronous motors to intervals above 1 year, the ability to accurately predict motor condition becomes critical. While significant literature exists on stator testing, comparatively little information is available to quantify the life of a synchronous rotor. Synchronous motors with salient poles will operate reliably for 25 years or more with proper care, but even the most durable motor will suffer rotor winding insulation breakdown after extended operation. As weak short-circuits in pole windings develop, increased excitation is required to maintain a given power factor and this additional rotor current increases heating, which accelerates the cumulative damage. This paper presents a selection of online and offline testing methods to provide the user with practical guidance on procedures and acceptance criteria to effectively quantify rotor turn to turn insulation. These methods provide a predictive tool to plan necessary repairs while maximizing the operational life of a synchronous motor.

articleTitle: Reducing pressure drop in pyro-processing
abstract: Pressure losses and poor particles' separation efficiencies increase Kcal/kg clinker. In some cases, as much as 20% raw feed exits with gas flow from the top cyclones, without being going through the heat recuperation process. The top cyclones require sophisticated design for lower pressure drop and higher particle separation operation. The firing of higher sulfur and chlorine containing fuels (i.e., pet-coke and AFR) in the calciners may also bring extra burden on ID fan through additional pressure losses and sometimes even kiln stoppages. The later problems are frequently observed in the lower cyclones and calciner/kiln hearth regions. The particles' collection efficiency in the top cyclones can be significantly improved with simple modifications to the meal entry design through detailed particles' dynamics analysis. The later issues in the lower cyclones and calciner can be diagnosed and rectified using detailed combustion and calcination interactive computational models. In this paper, some field data and case studies are presented where excessive pressure and feed losses, build-up issues were reduced. The presented results demonstrate innovative design modifications methodologies for obtaining flexible and attractive pay-back solutions.

articleTitle: 3D geologic modelling and mine planning to improve quarry and plant efficiency at cement operations
abstract: As mine operators encounter increasing opposition from regulators and public when permitting additional reserves, it is important for mining operations to maximize recovery of the permitted reserves in a cost effective manner. Effective planning at the mine can result in an extension of reserves, reduction in mining costs and reduction in plant maintenance costs. These results are achieved when a strategic mine plan, based upon the geology and limestone quality, is designed to maintain process control of raw limestone chemistry at the mine. The proposed mine planning method begins with the collection of geologic and quality data from exploration drilling and sampling. This information is utilized to construct a 3D geologic block model. Following block model creation, a strategic sequence of extraction is developed to deliver consistent raw limestone chemistry to the plant through blending and identify off-spec limestone to be sold at a lower value, beneficially reused or wasted at the mine. The challenges and engineered solutions associated with development of an operationally feasible mine plan is demonstrated through a case study of the 3D geologic modelling and mine planning method implemented at an active limestone quarry and cement plant operation.

articleTitle: Big data and its challenge for today's cement plant
abstract: Modern imaging devices can provide a wealth of information about the performance of a cement kiln, but that information is submerged in a far larger sea of raw data. Although the technology is familiar from consumer products, its effective use in a cement plant presents challenges for data transmission, storage, analysis and presentation. Both vendors and plant operators need to adapt to derive the full benefits.

articleTitle: The effect of raw material source on concrete duct bank thermal resistivity
abstract: Past experiments provided a method of determining concrete thermal resistivity using the constituents of the concrete mix. At that time material from only one source was used in the experiments. The question was raised whether the source of the sand or cement would affect the thermal resistivity of the concrete. This paper describes an experiment designed to determine whether the source of the sand and cement would affect the thermal resistivity of a concrete mix. The experiment performed determined that the source of the raw material will affect the thermal resistivity of concrete. This paper describes the experiment and includes the analysis of the gathered data. The experiment showed that the source from which both sand and cement was procured does have an effect on the final resistivity of concrete, and will affect the resistivity values that are used when determining the ampacity of cables encased in concrete duct banks.

articleTitle: Innovative oxygen injection for emission reduction in cement kilns
abstract: The reduction of CO and NO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">x</sub> from the cement process is a continued requirement for many cement manufacturers and often involves very expensive end-of-pipe pollution abatement solutions. The injection of highly reactive hot oxygen is a new approach that can be used to address lower emission requirements or complement under-performing existing solutions. The innovative oxygen lancing technology discussed in this paper is installed in the outlet of the kiln or calciner to address primarily CO from the system. Through careful excess oxygen reduction, the NO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">x</sub> generated in the main burner can be lowered as well because resulting CO can be oxidized with the oxygen injection. The technology consists of a lance that preheats oxygen to very high temperatures and effectively mixes this relatively small oxygen flow at high speed into much larger flue gas streams. The paper introduces the injection of oxygen into a cement kiln to reduce CO slip from the combustion process and includes data from a cement plant where the technology was implemented for the first time to simultaneously reduce CO and NO<sub xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">x</sub>.

articleTitle: Successful retrofit of a HPGR (High pressure grinding rolls) drive at a European cement company by replacing an existing electro-mechanical drive with a gearless direct Hydraulic drive
abstract: This paper describes the installation and operation of a success story for a retrofit of a HPGR drive replacing Electromechanical drive 2 × 500 kW with a direct Hydraulic drive using gearless Low Speed High Torque drive. This installation reduced the power required per ton of production, improved reliability and resistance to shock loads and faster response to torque fluctuation. Stabilize the challenge of nip adjustments and better consistency of finished product. This drive was commissioned during 2015. This paper provides details of drive configuration and steps involved and key factors considered and result of the performance improvement and productivity for grinding Clinker or Limestone.

articleTitle: The application and result of environmental initiatives at a commonwealth of Virginia Cement Plant
abstract: The cement plant's location, in the Roanoke Valley in the Commonwealth of Virginia, results from the presence of abundant limestone and other natural resources needed for cement production. The Troutville Plant's operations currently use about 100 acres of the 2,500 acres on its campus. Its vision is to be recognized as a leading enterprise in its industry for sustainability and environmental stewardship. A long-term energy management project resulted in impressive energy savings. Environmental reclamation projects turned problem areas into nature attractions. It implements this vision by constantly monitoring its environmental performance and continually making improvements. The ENERGY STAR® designation every year for the past 11 years is reflective of this effort.

articleTitle: Foundations design of multiple vertical mills focused on vibration mitigation
abstract: In this work a computational procedure for evaluating the dynamic effects of multiple vertical mills operating simultaneously is presented and discussed. In this regard, the effect of different parameters such as soils dynamic properties, vertical mills proximity and the damping parameter of the involved soils are evaluated. The aim of the presented procedure is the accurate evaluation of the effects of the operations of multiple vertical mills on the resulting vibrations in their foundations and in other buildings in the proximity. Based on this, the most appropriate design measurements may be adopted with the purpose to mitigate the resulting vibrations during the simultaneous operation of multiple vertical mills. To demonstrate the capabilities of the proposed computational procedure for evaluating the resulting vibrations during the simultaneous operations of vertical mills, numerical results related to real cases of cement plants are presented, where the foundations of the existing multiple vertical mills were designed following the numerical procedure detailed in this work.

articleTitle: Increasing pyro system productivity through innovative preheater upgrades
abstract: Introducing new pyro process technologies into existing cement plant operations to increase productivity is vital for maintaining the sustainability of cement plants in economically competitive market conditions. This paper presents a case study of collaboration between an equipment supplier and a cement producer in developing, engineering, performing industrial trials for and optimizing new technologies into an existing preheater in two phases during the plant's annual planned shutdowns in two successive years. The performance results summarized in this paper show an improvement from the upgrades to the top-stage cyclone of the preheater. The success from this project allows the plant to operate at increased capacity with savings to specific fuel consumption. With this technology proven, the cement produce has incorporated the new top-stage cyclone into a new production line with benefits due to reduced preheater civil and structural requirements.

articleTitle: The friction compensator — Visualizing refractory expansion
abstract: An increasing number of damages observed on calciner steel shells are a direct result of a volume increase of the refractory lining. Over years of operation, mineralogical alkali effects are mainly the cause. The thermal expansion of the refractory lining is a physical process and can be calculated and foreseen with the refractory engineering. However, volume increase due to mineralogical phenomena of refractory materials needs special attention. In order to compensate for expansion of the lining, various expansion joints are positioned in the refractory lining. These expansion joints have to be controlled, cleaned and, if necessary, filled with new expansion joint material. When neglected, expansion joints will be closed and will not fulfil their task anymore. As a result, structural damages of the calciner vessels and cyclones can be observed in several clinker burning lines worldwide. With a friction compensator, the plant operator now has a tool to determine and measure the expansion of the refractory lining, especially in calciners, without the need to interrupt production. An inspection of the expansion joints from inside the vessel is not necessary and the planning of repair measures will become easier.

articleTitle: Application of next-generation motor management relays to improve system reliability in process industries
abstract: This paper describes advances in functionality of motor management relays in terms of both motor protection and predictive diagnostics. Network connectivity of these devices via high-speed Ethernet-IP allows real-time monitoring of system parameters, providing analytics to allow process industry users to better manage system processes to improve reliability, efficiency and safety. A case study of a recent application of new motor management relays in included in the paper, offering producers a specific example of how new motor management relays are applied and outlining details involved to leverage the latest technologies.

articleTitle: Hydrocarbon testing & emissions in cement plants
abstract: The total hydrocarbon emissions from cement kilns have come under regulation over the past several years. The EPA's National Emission Standards for Hazardous Air Pollutants (NESHAP) has put a cap of 24 ppmvdc (parts per million on a volumetric basic, dry gas, and corrected to standard conditions) on total hydrocarbon (THC) emissions. THCs are easy to measure and are felt to be an indicator of combustion efficiency, by the EPA. However, unlike other industries, THC emissions in cement plants can come from both combustion and raw materials. This paper documents common sources of THC emissions in cement manufacture. The paper uses experiences from different cement plants to document testing procedures and results that assist in understanding THC emissions. Understanding the sources of THC emissions is the first step in developing a mitigation and compliance strategy. The paper also reviews some of the more common THC emission control technologies that can be used. Some of the advantages and disadvantages of these technologies are provided. The result is a road map that can be followed by other cement plants in diagnosing and resolving THC emissions issues and maintaining compliance with air regulations on a continuous basis.

articleTitle: Computational fluid dynamics simulation in the cement manufacturing process
abstract: New technologies continue to enter the workforce that when properly utilized can significantly improve operational and manufacturing practices. Computational Fluid Dynamics (CFD) simulation and Bulk Flow Modeling are two such technologies showing great promise in both the cement manufacturing and the more general building materials industries. Whether used as a tool through an engineering contractor or brought in-house, cement manufacturers should utilize Computational Fluid Dynamics simulation to capitalize on all opportunities to improve processes. Potential improvements include but are not limited to reduced energy consumption, reduced wear on equipment, and improved material distribution to key equipment. This paper will serve as an introduction to the capabilities of both Computational Fluid Dynamics and Bulk Flow Modeling and will showcase potential applications in cement manufacturing plants. This paper will also demonstrate the value of Computational Fluid Dynamics simulation through two case studies, including one that ultimately reduced resource consumption.

articleTitle: Back to basics-troubleshooting a synchronous motor issue in a cement plant
abstract: A case study detailing some of the challenges, trials and tribulations when troubleshooting a problem with a 2250 HP synchronous mill motor in a cement plant. The first sign of a problem came after the replacement of the mill motor starter and synchronous starter. The plant was having operational issues with the motor reaching synchronous speed and dropping out before synchronizing. This paper will detail the methodology and effort to resolve this problem.

articleTitle: Challenges of a new quarry five miles from a plant
abstract: This document is a case study outlining the electrical challenges faced by an international cement producer when interfacing a new quarry located approximately five miles from the existing plant. The existing quarry adjacent to the plant has nearly exhausted the limestone natural resource prominent in cement production. After studying several options, the corporation concluded a five mile long conveying system to be the most economical and stable long term solution for transporting stone from the new quarry to the plant. The longest single portion of the new conveyor is approximately 4.5 miles long. With limited rural electrical power available it was most efficient to utilize power from the existing plant to feed the new quarry. Electrical challenges faced include voltage drop, coordination of variable frequency drives approximately 4.5 miles apart, wireless mobile management at the crusher in the new quarry, voice and data communications along the conveyor, five miles of control and safety interlocks, and four new substations to be installed in remote locations.

articleTitle: [Front cover]
abstract: The following topics are dealt with: cement industry; industrial plants; maintenance engineering; kilns; cements (building materials); combustion; air pollution control; calcination; steel; cost reduction.
